input: Get a pollinator-friendly plant list from a local nursery

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Pollinators vary widely — bees, butterflies, hummingbirds, moths — and the plant list changes significantly depending on which ones the user wants to attract.
Knowing whether this list is for the user alone or to share with others (e.g., a community group, school, HOA) affects how detailed or formatted the list needs to be.
The planting environment — sun exposure, garden size, region/climate — determines which plants the nursery should recommend and whether the list will actually be usable.
A budget limit shapes how many plants the user intends to buy from the list, which may affect how long or specific the list needs to be.
Some users want only native plants, others are open to non-natives or specific aesthetics (color, height, bloom season), which narrows or broadens what the nursery should include.
Whether the user plans to visit in person, call, or email the nursery determines the immediate next action and how to prepare for the interaction.
The user may want a simple verbal list, a written handout, or a detailed guide with care instructions — knowing this defines what a successful outcome looks like.

gold.taskTitle: Get pollinator-friendly plant list from local nursery
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to obtain a curated list of pollinator-friendly plants from a nearby nursery, likely to guide a planting or gardening project.

questions.title: Which pollinators are you most trying to attract?
questions.description: Identify the target pollinators — bees, butterflies, hummingbirds, moths, or a general mix — so the nursery can tailor their recommendations accordingly.

questions.title: Is this list just for you or others too?
questions.description: Clarify whether the plant list is for personal use or intended to be shared with a group, which affects the needed level of detail and formatting.

questions.title: What are the sun and space conditions of your planting area?
questions.description: Determine the garden's physical conditions — sun exposure, soil type, available space, and geographic region — so the recommendations will be regionally and environmentally appropriate.

questions.title: Do you have a budget in mind for purchasing plants?
questions.description: Establish a rough spending limit so the nursery can suggest a realistic number of plants and the user knows how selective to be from the list.

questions.title: Do you prefer native plants over non-native varieties?
questions.description: Find out whether the user wants strictly native species, is open to non-natives, or has preferences around bloom color, height, or season that should shape the list.

questions.title: Will you visit, call, or email the nursery for this?
questions.description: Determine the contact method so the immediate next action can be clearly defined — e.g., preparing questions to ask in person vs. drafting an email inquiry.

questions.title: What should the final plant list actually include?
questions.description: Define what a complete, useful list looks like to the user — a quick verbal rundown, a written list of names, or a detailed guide with care and bloom information.
